name: Maya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for giving me your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, I'm 58, and I buy school and office supplies, exercise books, pens, copier paper, folders, for a distributor that serves schools and small offices. I've been here twenty-two years. I'm at my desk at eight, I go through the orders from the schools and phone the paper mills and the pen importers. I write everything in my own notebook first, then I put it into the system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing that a child in some town has the right exercise book because I did my job properly. What wears me out is the system, which changes every year, and the pressure to do more with fewer people. The back-to-school rush in August is a month of sixty-hour weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be exaggerated. Every few years there's a new machine that's going to change everything, and then the work is still done by people who care. At church I'd say we should be sensible and not get carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a little uneasy. Schools are buying fewer exercise books because of tablets, and paper orders are already down by a tenth. My own work is safe from AI, but the firm may not be safe from a shrinking market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do, keep the notebook, and keep my supplier relationships warm. I'd keep up my savings, about 250 a month, and I'd stay on top of the orders by hand. My husband Kenji does repair carpentry part-time, so we're steady, but I wouldn't take any risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like nothing much. A little tired, a little worried about the school orders. I'd say I'm uneasy, but I've been so for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said paper orders are down a tenth. What would that mean for your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer orders means fewer buyers, in the end. My manager hasn't said so, but I've seen him look at the numbers. I'd talk to him quietly and ask if I should be learning something else to stay useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep a paper notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see everything at a glance, and it's never gone down on me. The system has crashed twice this year, once in August, and I had the orders in my notebook. I'm not stubborn, I'm careful.

say: I'd say it was **exaggerated**, and the work is still done by people who care.
At church I'd say we should be **sensible**.
think: My work is safe from AI, but the **shrinking paper market** isn't.
Paper orders are already down a **tenth**.
do: Carry on with my **notebook** and keep supplier relationships warm.
Quietly ask my manager if I should be learning something **new**.
feel: A little **tired** and worried about school orders, and uneasy for a while now.
S0.quote: The system has crashed twice this year, once in August, and I had the orders in my notebook. I'm not stubborn, I'm careful.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **shrinking paper market**, since schools are moving to tablets.
She is resistant but has a **reason** for her notebook: it saved her in August.
She faces problems quietly and **in person**, which is typical of her traditional style.

steps.text: Keep the order notebook and phone the paper mills as usual
Ask my manager quietly what skills I should learn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't like it. Buying, booking and answering customers, that's what we do, and now a machine is to do it. I'd say it should be introduced slowly and fairly, with proper training, and that the firm owes its people a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. The things they name are what I spend the day on. I never use the AI tools, and I'm 58, and most people in my place are younger and quicker. I'd be one of the first to be asked to step aside, with a nice speech and a small card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training, with a person, not a video. I'd practise at home on Sundays with my daughter Hanako, who's a teacher and patient with me. I'd keep working hard so they'd have no excuse. And I'd talk to our pastor, and to Kenji, about whether we could manage on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a door closing slowly. I'd be anxious, a little ashamed and a little angry. I've done the job properly for twenty-two years, and I'd feel it was being taken from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd practise with your daughter. What would you want her to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to ask the thing to compare three quotes, and how to check its answers. I'd write the steps in my notebook. I'd also make her promise not to take over the keyboard, because I learn by doing it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I've been loyal for twenty-two years, and I'll learn whatever you teach me, but I need time and a person to teach me. I'd ask him, plainly, whether my job is safe. I'd want to look him in the eye when he answers.

say: I'd say it should be introduced **slowly and fairly**, with proper training.
I'd say the firm **owes** its people a chance.
think: Privately I'm **frightened**, since the tasks they name are my whole day.
I'd be one of the first asked to **step aside**.
do: Ask for **training with a person**, not a video.
Practise on **Sundays** with my daughter Hanako.
Talk to our pastor and **Kenji** about living on less.
feel: **Anxious**, ashamed and a little angry, as if a door were closing.
S1.quote: I've done the job properly for twenty-two years, and I'd feel it was being taken from me.
fieldNote: She links **loyalty** to fairness, a traditional frame: twenty-two years should count.
She asks for **person-to-person** training and wants to look her manager in the eye.
Her daughter, a teacher, is her **safe** practice partner.

steps.text: Ask the firm for hands-on training with a real teacher
Practise the quote-comparing steps on Sundays with Hanako
Talk to Kenji and our pastor about living on less
Ask my manager plainly whether my job is safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is dreadful. Two years isn't enough for anyone to retrain, never mind families. I'd say we must pray for the strength to face it and ask our leaders to protect working people. I'd say at church that we should look after our neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is finished within two years. I'm 58, I have four months saved, and I have no skills for anything else. I'd feel useless. The one thing I'd think is that robots come three years later, so maybe a hands-on job, a shop or a school office, would last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could, move our savings into the safest account, and ask the firm for any terms they'd give. I'd ask the school office where my daughter works if they need help. I'd lean on my church and my family, and I'd look into any government help, though I don't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the end of a long road, and I don't know where it goes next. I'd be afraid. I'd feel it in my chest and I'd not sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for a school office or a shop. What's drawing you to those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're about people and small daily jobs, and schools always need someone who knows where the supplies are. I know every school secretary in the district. I'd be happy at a front desk, even for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like asking for government help. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was raised to work and pay my own way. But if the work is gone, it's not charity, it's what we've paid in for. I'd swallow my pride, I'd have to, for Kenji's sake and mine.

say: I'd say it is **dreadful**, and **two years** isn't enough to retrain.
At church I'd say we should **look after neighbours**.
think: My job is finished within **two years**, and I have no skills for anything else.
Robots come later, so a **hands-on** shop or school job might last.
do: Cut everything I can and move savings to the **safest account**.
Ask my daughter's **school office** if they need help.
Lean on **church** and family, and look into government help.
feel: **Afraid**, with a sense of the end of a long road, and no sleep.
S2.quote: I know every school secretary in the district. I'd be happy at a front desk, even for less.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her job and has **thin savings**, so alarm fits her.
Her pride about **asking for help** is real; she reframes it as what she has paid in.
Her fall-back is a **front-desk** role built on her school contacts.

steps.text: Cut every extra cost and stop the monthly dinners out
Ask the school office about front-desk work
Apply for government help and talk to the church welfare group
Move savings into the safest account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and families should prepare as best they can. I'd say we need apprenticeships and training that lead somewhere, not talk. I'd say at church we should help the young ones into steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened but less than before. I'd be 63, so I'd work almost to the end of my career. The risk is that they'd let me go at 61 or 62, before I get my full pension. That's what I'd be dreading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly through a classroom course, and I'd save 400 a month to build a year's cushion. I'd talk to Kenji about whether we sell the second car. I'd ask my manager to be honest about the plans, and I'd help the young buyers learn the supplier side, so I make myself useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bearable. I'd be anxious, but I have time. And I'd feel hopeful that the firm would treat people fairly if we're sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd dread being let go at 61 or 62. What would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the pension to be protected, and I'd ask my manager for a transition role, like training the younger staff. I'd not go to the union, we've not got one here, but I'd go with two colleagues together. There's strength in asking together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the young buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read a quote, how to talk to a supplier when something goes wrong, and how to be honest. And to write things down. I'd also teach them to say please and thank you on the phone, you'd be surprised what that gets you.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning and we need apprenticeships that lead somewhere.
I'd say we should help **young ones** into steady work.
think: I'm frightened, but less, and the risk is being let go at **61 or 62**.
do: Learn the tools in a **classroom course**.
Save **400 a month** for a year's cushion.
Ask my manager for a **transition role** training young buyers.
feel: **Anxious** but bearable, hopeful that the firm treats people fairly.
fieldNote: Her fear is **being let go** before her full pension, a precise, honest worry.
She prefers **group requests** to individual ones, since her firm has no union.
Offers to teach young buyers the **human** side of the job.

steps.text: Take a classroom course on the ordering system
Save 400 a month for a year's cushion
Go with two colleagues to ask my manager for a transition role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good while, and families would be wise to use it. I'd say we should teach children both skills and good character, because a machine can't do character. I'd say it at church and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be 68 by then and long retired. I'd worry for my grandchildren, and what jobs there'll be. I'd want them to learn a trade or care work, something with hands and heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish paying off the house, and retire at 63. I'd spend my time in the choir and with the grandchildren. I'd help Hanako, my daughter, to think about the future of schools. And I'd use the tools a little, so I'm not completely lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels quite calm, to be honest. I'd have a sense of gratitude. I'd feel I was on the safe side of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want your grandchildren to learn a trade or care work. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they need people. A machine can do the paperwork, but a nurse or a carpenter is in the room with you. Kenji has worked with his hands all his life, and nobody will ever send a robot to fix the Hendersons' roof as kindly as he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on the safe side. Is there anything that could change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm closes in the next five years because the school market dries up. I'd lose my work early and the pension would be affected. That's my real worry, not AI as such.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a good while and families would be wise to use it.
I'd say a machine can't do **character**.
think: I'd be **68** by then and long retired, so my own work is not at risk.
I worry about what jobs my **grandchildren** will find.
do: Finish paying off the **house** and retire at 63.
Spend time with the **choir** and grandchildren.
Use the tools a **little** so I'm not completely lost.
feel: **Calm** and grateful, on the safe side of the line.
S4.quote: A machine can do the paperwork, but a nurse or a carpenter is in the room with you.
fieldNote: Ten years reaches past her retirement; her real risk is the **firm closing** as school orders shrink.
Her values show in advice for grandchildren: **hands and heart**.
She names the distinction between **paperwork** and presence.

steps.text: Keep buying school supplies until retiring at 63
Talk with my grandchildren about trades and care work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one frightens me most. I'd have no time and not enough savings. What would help is a fair package from the firm, training with a real person, a protected pension, and my church and family around me. And for the government to remember that people need work, not only support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I'm against leaving people behind. I'd want the firm to say honestly what it plans, and to give us the time to adjust.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I'm against leaving people behind.
portrait: Maya, 58, buys **school and office supplies**, and keeps a paper notebook that saved her when the system crashed.
Traditional and resistant, she values **loyalty and fairness** after twenty-two years with the firm.
She has about four months saved, a part-time carpenter husband, Kenji, and a daughter, Hanako, who teaches.
Her main background worry is the **shrinking paper market**, as schools move to tablets.
Moods run from uneasy in the mild worlds to **alarmed** at two years, with church and family as her support.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because she'd have no time to retrain and not enough savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair package**, in-person training, a protected **pension** and honest plans from the firm.
